title: Proxy: External Proxy
summary: An external proxy is a relay that sits outside the victim environment, typically on purchased cloud resources or a virtual private server, and forwards traffic from compromised hosts to the real command and control server. Victim systems connect only to that intermediary, so blocking the known control address removes nothing, and the operator can move the real server without touching a single implant. Port redirectors are a common implementation, and proxies are often chosen because a connection from the victim environment to them is unlikely to be investigated. Detection combines connection metadata with context: new external destinations on hosts that have no business reason to reach them, consistent beacon intervals, long sessions to one address, and the same proxy address appearing in the logs of many unrelated systems inside the estate.

beginner.definition: This is a proxy that sits outside your network, usually on a rented server on the internet. Your infected computers connect to that outside server. It then forwards the traffic to the real control server. Unlike the parent technique, which covers middle machines of any kind, this sub-technique is about relays on the internet.
beginner.whyItMatters: Blocking the attacker's known server does not help if traffic goes to a middle server first. The attacker can change the real server without touching your computers. Rented servers are cheap, so this setup is easy to replace. The middle server may also look like a normal website or online service. You need to look at how the traffic behaves, not only at where it goes.
howItWorks: The attacker rents a server or buys cloud resources somewhere on the internet.
They set it up to forward incoming traffic to the real control server.
Infected computers are configured to contact the rented server rather than the real one.
The rented server relays the traffic and hides the true destination from your network.
The attacker can replace the real server while the infected computers keep working.
Defenders detect new external destinations, steady beacon timing and address reuse across hosts.
beginner.example: Imagine ordering a parcel to a locker in another city, then paying a courier to bring it to your real address. Anyone watching your street sees only the courier. If you move house, the locker still works and the courier simply delivers somewhere else. An external proxy is that locker, and stopping one courier does not close it.
takeaways: Blocking one address rarely stops traffic that travels through a relay.
Regular timing from many hosts to a new external address is a red flag.
Share intelligence about relay addresses across the whole estate.

objectives: Explain what an external proxy is and where it usually sits.
Describe how port redirection forwards control traffic.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from an internal proxy.
Identify the network logs and metadata that reveal external relaying.
Describe why blocking a single destination address is not sufficient.
